source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design: distance, commonness, modality of examples
finding: Far-field patent examples gave more novel ideas than near-field examples and a wider spread of idea quality, but fewer ideas. Mean and max quality did not differ. Far examples did not beat the no-example control on novelty.
numbers: N=153 senior engineering students, 9 cells (distance x commonness x modality) plus control. Far vs near: solution transfer d=0.60; quantity d=-0.30 (about one idea fewer); quality SD d=0.64 vs near, 0.78 vs control; mean novelty d=0.56; max novelty d=0.56; breadth no effect (p=.78).
limits: One problem (rural energy harvesting), one session, examples shown after a first ideation phase. Far-vs-control novelty gap not significant by itself.
agent_relevance: Far hints help by moving to a new region, but cost time. Use them as a variance booster, not a mean-quality booster.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design: distance, commonness, modality of examples
finding: Less-common examples (rarely seen designs) raised novelty and widened quality spread without hurting quantity. The effect came from broader search, not copying.
numbers: Less-common vs more-common: mean novelty d=0.61, max novelty d=0.61, quality SD d=0.62 (vs control 0.68), quantity d=0.67 higher than more-common, breadth d=0.61. More-common examples cut breadth vs control (d=-1.03) and quantity (d=-0.76). Far-field AND less-common combined beat control: mean novelty d=1.14, max d=1.29 (Dunnett post hoc).
limits: Commonness was rated by judges for these patents only; the combined cell is a post hoc contrast.
agent_relevance: Rarity of the hint matters separately from distance. Hints that are well-known pull the model to typical solutions (see G4: samples not independent). Prefer hints the model would not produce by default.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design: distance, commonness, modality of examples
finding: Picture versus text format of the example changed copying and quantity but not the final novelty or quality spread.
numbers: Text examples gave more solution transfer (d=0.60) and about two fewer ideas than picture or control (d=-0.67 vs picture, -0.56 vs control). Modality on mean novelty p=.20, max novelty p=.49, quality SD p=.44.
limits: Students, patents only.
agent_relevance: Format of the stimulus is a weak lever. Do not spend scaffold effort on it.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design: distance, commonness, modality of examples
finding: Mechanism split: far examples worked through solution transfer with lower quantity (go deep in one new region); less-common examples worked through breadth and higher quantity. The authors read the lower quantity under far as mapping time cost: after removing the example-processing phase the quantity effect vanished (p=.47).
numbers: Final-phase quantity effect of distance p=.47; commonness effect remained p<.05, d=0.56. Process model correlations all p<.01.
limits: Correlational process model; causal paths not tested.
agent_relevance: Two separate operators: one that maps a distant case in depth (costly), one that widens search with unusual cases (cheaper). Budget the mapping cost explicitly.

source: Fu, Chan, Cagan, Kotovsky, Schunn, Wood (2013) The meaning of near and far: structuring design databases and effect of distance of analogy on design output
finding: Failed to reproduce the 2011 far advantage. With patents placed on a computed similarity structure, far stimuli gave LESS novel and LOWER quality ideas than near stimuli or no stimuli.
numbers: N=72 enrolled, 70 analysed (24 near, 24 far, 24 control; 10 graduate, 62 undergraduate). Max novelty F(2,59)=4.14, p=.02; far lower than near d=0.82 (p=.02) and control d=0.91 (p=.008). Mean novelty F(2,61)=1.63, p=.20 (same direction). Mean quality F(2,65)=4.07, p=.02; near higher than far d=0.76; near vs control d=0.54 (p=.23, n.s.). Max quality F(2,65)=4.13, p=.02. Quantity p=.94, breadth p=.62.
limits: Single problem, 15-minute task, 5 near and 5 far patents with 3 shown per person. Far patents were rated significantly less relevant by participants (Fig. 5).
agent_relevance: Clear boundary condition. Far hints can hurt when the model or person cannot map them. Gate far hints on a relevance or mappability check.

source: Fu et al. (2013), same paper: reconciliation of the 2011 and 2013 studies
finding: The authors put the stimuli of both studies on one patent-structure map. Near and far are relative. The 2011 near set was too near to help; the 2013 far set was too far to help. They propose a sweet spot at intermediate distance.
numbers: Distance measured in nodes on a patent structure: near = 0 or 1 node, far = 3 nodes from the problem. The sweet spot is stated as dependent on problem and patent set.
quote: there is such a thing as too far
limits: The inverted-U is an inference from two studies and a map, not from a graded distance experiment in one sample. Authors call stabilising the sweet spot future work.
agent_relevance: Do not hard-code far is better. Treat distance as a tunable parameter and measure the payoff on a held-out check (G3).

source: Chan, Dow, Schunn (2014) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? Design Studies
finding: Large field test on the OpenIDEO site. Concepts that cited sources were more likely to be shortlisted than concepts that cited none, and among citers, nearer sources went with better outcomes. The inverse distance effect held in every one of 12 challenges.
numbers: 2341 concepts, 12 challenges, 1190 contributors; 707 concepts cited at least one source (2245 sources); 110 of 707 (16%) shortlisted by expert panel. Cross-classified logistic models: AIC baseline 511.39, with max-distance 506.04, with mean-distance 505.13. Author and challenge variance 0.44 and 0.50 (ICC about .11 and .13).
limits: Correlational, only cited sources counted, outcome is expert shortlist (blends novelty and usefulness). Social-innovation problems only. Authors say highly creative ideas can also come from far sources.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence against the leap hypothesis at scale. Default the agent to near-to-moderate analogues and use far ones sparingly.

source: Chan, Dow, Schunn (2014) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? Design Studies
finding: The paper's literature review shows mixed support for far sources and names the power problem: most earlier experiments had 12 or fewer per cell.
numbers: Only four earlier studies had 18+ per cell (Chan 2011, Fu 2013, Goncalves 2013, Tseng 2008), split evenly for and against far. Dahl and Moreau (2002) correlational, 119 participants. Enkel and Gassmann (2010) 25 cases.
limits: Review is by authors who are partly the opponents of the leap hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Treat single-study far-analogy wins (and LLM demos built on them) as weak. Ask for replication before building an operator on them.

source: Chan, Dow, Schunn (2014) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? Design Studies
finding: Reported in the review (primary papers not opened): Tseng et al. 2008 found far sources helped more after ideation began; Wilson et al. 2010 found no far advantage on novelty and near sources cut idea variety; Hender 2002 reported a quantity cost of far sources.
numbers: As summarised by Chan, Dow, Schunn 2014. No numbers given in the summary.
limits: Second-hand; primary papers not read this session.
agent_relevance: Timing matters: give analogues after the model has produced its own first drafts, not before.

source: Chan, Dow, Schunn (2014) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? Design Studies
finding: Rival explanations offered for the outsider advantage seen in practice: (1) expertise in the far domain lets people map it cheaply; (2) outsiders bring different problem representations; (3) outsiders are less attached to the status quo. The paper says no study directly tests the expertise-mediation account.
numbers: Hargadon and Sutton (1997) IDEO ethnography fits expertise-mediation. No effect sizes.
limits: Theory section; speculative.
agent_relevance: Distance alone is not the active ingredient. A far analogue may need a domain-expert pass (a specialised prompt or retrieval of source-domain structure) to pay off.

source: Chan and Schunn (2014) The impact of analogies on creative concept generation: lessons from an in vivo cognitive science study of design. Cognitive Science
finding: In a professional team's real brainstorming, concepts that followed a far analogy were NOT further from their predecessor than baseline concepts. They were slightly more incremental. Far analogies did not produce jumps.
numbers: 144 analogies found across two transcripts. Study 1 distance coded on a 1-5 overlap scale. Result robust across window sizes and measures.
limits: One team, one project, hand-coded; low generality.
agent_relevance: The assumed mechanism (far analogy gives big jump) is not supported. Do not expect a far hint to produce a distant idea; expect deeper local exploration.

source: Chan and Schunn (2014) The impact of analogies on creative concept generation: lessons from an in vivo cognitive science study of design. Cognitive Science
finding: Far analogies raised the team's concept generation rate (fluency), not lowered it. So the incremental pattern is not simple fixation.
limits: Small variance explained. Coding by hand.
agent_relevance: Far analogies may act as fuel for sustained exploration of one functional space. Use them to extend a branch, not to start a new one.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999) Analogical encoding facilitates knowledge transfer in negotiation
finding: Comparing two cases side by side (analogical encoding) raised transfer of the shared strategy, in novices and in graduate managers. Studying the same cases separately did not.
numbers: Exp 1A baseline: 94% (15/16) wrote compromises, 19% tradeoff, 0% contingency. Exp 1B with analogy training: tradeoff 38%, contingency 69% (11/16). Exp 2: MBA students who compared two cases were nearly three times as likely to use the strategy as those given the same cases separately.
limits: Negotiation, not design. Small cells (16 per cell in Exp 1).
agent_relevance: Supports an operator that makes the agent compare two analogues and write the shared principle before applying it, rather than reading one analogue.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson, Gentner (1999), background figures on retrieval vs use
finding: Foundational pattern: people retrieve by surface match but judge usefulness by relational match. Without a hint, spontaneous analogy use is low.
numbers: Gentner et al. 1993 as reported: surface-match stories recalled 55% vs 12% for purely analogical matches, yet only relational matches rated useful for inference. Gick and Holyoak radiation problem: about 10% solve unaided; 41% apply the fortress analogy spontaneously; about 85% when told to think about the earlier problem.
limits: Numbers are second-hand through this paper.
agent_relevance: Far analogues fail at retrieval, not at use. An agent should retrieve by function or structure (a rewritten problem), not by topic words.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer (as cited by Loewenstein et al. 1999)
finding: Dissociation between retrieval and inference: retrieval driven by surface similarity, inference driven by relational similarity.
numbers: 55% recall for surface-matched stories vs 12% for analogy-only matches, as quoted in Loewenstein et al.
limits: Not opened; second hand.
agent_relevance: Same as above.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining. KDD
finding: Retrieving analogues by learned purpose-and-mechanism vectors, instead of surface text similarity, raised the share of good ideas in a human ideation experiment.
numbers: 749 ideas total. With seeds common to all 3 conditions (9 seeds), k=2 judges: 46% good (n=105) vs random 37% (49) vs TF-IDF surface 30% (54), p<.01. k=3: 38% vs 22% vs 21%. Mixed model k=2: pr(good)=0.71 [0.48,0.87] vs 0.28 (TF-IDF) and 0.27 (random); chi2(3)=67.96. Judge agreement Fleiss kappa 0.51. Phase design: 1 min unaided then 6 min with 12 inspirations.
limits: Crowd workers, one redesign task type, judged by 5 graduate students; model learned on product descriptions.
agent_relevance: Best-controlled retrieval result. Notable: surface-near (TF-IDF) was no better than random. Retrieve by purpose plus mechanism schema, then apply.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2023/2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: LLMs recognise near analogies but fail on far analogies where surface overlap is absent. Far analogy with a near distractor is the worst case.
numbers: Zero-shot, 50% chance. Humans 96% overall; near analogies 97.9% human vs 75.0% model average; far analogies 94.1% human vs 39.6% model (below chance). (far,far) 45.3%; far analogy vs near distractor 33.9%. GPT-4 below random on far analogies. SBERT surface baseline 77.9% on near. Annotator kappa 0.865 on 120 items. Few-shot plus chain of thought helped; best model about halfway between random and human.
limits: Models of 2023 vintage (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2, FlanT5, UnifiedQA, Macaw). Narratives from ePiC proverbs, elements extracted by GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of the near/far split. Our agent should not trust itself to pick a far analogue over a surface-similar one. Add a structural check (map roles) before use.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on matrix, letter-string and verbal analogies, but on story analogies it was clearly worse than students, and not significant in the far condition.
numbers: Story analogies: GPT-3 binomial p=.0005 overall, near p=.0039, far p=.065 (not significant); humans N=54 all p<1e-22. Humans better than GPT-3: OR=0.37, p=.0003, CI [0.21,0.63]. 15 of 54 students always chose the analogous story. Other samples: matrix N=40, letter-string N=57, verbal N=57. GPT-4 preliminary: stronger, near perfect on near.
limits: GPT-3 and early GPT-4. Contamination worry: story items come from a published 1980s study.
agent_relevance: Far story analogy is where LLMs lag; scaling helps, but see the robustness check next.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Replication of Webb et al. Original results reproduce, but on variants (permuted or symbol alphabets, moved blank, paraphrased stories, swapped answer order) GPT performance drops sharply while humans hold steady. Evidence of reliance on training-like patterns.
numbers: Letter-string human samples: 276 (0 generalisations), 138, 92, 92. GPT-3 reproduces Webb; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 slightly lower. Story analogies: GPT-4 was 89% (16/18) when story A was right but 61% (11/18) when story B was right, an answer-order bias. Shortcut found: correct story often more similar at sentence level.
limits: Study covers 3 of 4 domains of Webb. Small 18-item story set. Authors note humans also poor on complex problems.
agent_relevance: Failed-robustness result. Never accept one-order, one-wording agreement as proof of analogy skill (G3, G4). Swap order and paraphrase when testing analogues.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: On a 24K story-pair corpus annotated for entity similarity and relation similarity, analogy identification is very hard for embeddings and LLMs. Sentence encoders track entity similarity better than relation similarity.
numbers: ChatGPT about 30% on multiple choice vs over 85% for humans. Fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl on the corpus matches zero-shot ChatGPT on analogy generation. 24K pairs, EntSim and RelSim scored 0 to 3.
limits: Multiple-choice task design drives the low accuracy; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Embedding similarity is a surface-near retriever. Relation-level matching needs a separate step.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: InstructGPT can generate analogous source concepts for a target. Best prompts are imperative statements at low temperature. The largest model reaches human-level on producing a meaningful analogue; explaining the similarity is weaker.
numbers: Human evaluation on 1.4k generated analogies; quality rises with model size. Sensitive to question vs imperative wording and to spelling errors.
limits: Evaluation of meaningful, not of usefulness for any design task. Concept pairs are science-textbook style.
agent_relevance: Generating analogues is cheap for LLMs. The bottleneck is mapping and judging usefulness, not producing candidates.

source: Yasunaga, Chen, Li, Pasupat, Leskovec, Liang, Chi, Zhou (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners. ICLR
finding: Prompting a model to recall its own relevant problems before solving beat zero-shot and, on several tasks, few-shot chain of thought. These are near, self-generated analogues, not far ones.
numbers: Codeforces GPT-3.5-turbo Acc@1: 0-shot 8, CoT 9, 3-shot 11, self-exemplars 13, +knowledge 15; GPT-4: 16, 16, 17, 17, 19. GSM8K GPT-3.5: 77.8 self-generated with diversity vs 75.9 without; MATH 37.3 vs 35.2; with self-consistency 85.3 and 46.0. BIG-Bench word sorting 66.8 (0-shot) to 75.2. K=1 to 5 exemplars: GSM8K 76.1 to 77.8. Manual audit of 50 correct: 6 irrelevant exemplars, 9 relevant but wrong, 35 good.
limits: Same-task analogues (math, code), not cross-domain design. Gains small; 3-shot CoT wins on temporal sequences (58.0 vs 57.6).
agent_relevance: Self-generated near analogues give a modest, reliable gain at low cost. Asking for diversity helped. The only LLM result here with a clean gain, and it is near-analogy.

source: Zhu and Luo (2023) Biologically inspired design concept generation using generative pre-trained transformers (with Zhu and Luo 2022 Generative transformers for design concept generation)
finding: Fine-tuned GPT-3 generators retrieve a biological analogue and map it to an engineering problem, tested on flying-car design. Evaluated by fine-tuned relevance classifiers and one team review; no human control group.
numbers: 50 concepts per generator for each of 3 robot samples; semantic distance by word-mover's distance; case study on a light-weight flying car with a design team. The 2022 companion paper (arXiv 2211.03468) adds analogy-driven synthesis, evaluated by human and data-driven scoring.
limits: No head-to-head against human designers or against a no-hint baseline. Machine evaluators are themselves fine-tuned models, so circular.
agent_relevance: Feasibility demo only. No evidence yet that LLM-supplied far analogies improve design outcomes (G3 applies).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study
finding: Not analogy specific, but the best controlled test of LLM ideation vs experts. LLM ideas judged more novel and slightly less feasible. The LLM agent's idea pool collapses to few distinct ideas.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 49 ideas per condition. Novelty score human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (AI vs human p<.05). From 4000 generated seed ideas only about 200 (5%) were non-duplicate at cosine 0.8. LLM self-evaluation failed as a ranker.
limits: Research ideas in NLP, not design. Novelty judged on paper, not executed.
agent_relevance: Our hint-generation stage should expect low diversity: sampling more from one model gives repeats (G4). Diversity of analogues must be forced by structure, not by temperature.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL benchmark for long-text analogy
finding: Across a six-level taxonomy from word to metaphor, eight LLMs find it harder to identify analogous pairs as the level rises.
numbers: 13 datasets, 3 distance measures, 8 LLMs, embedding-space identification.
limits: Embedding-based, not generative; only the abstract and setup were read.
agent_relevance: More abstract analogies need more than embedding retrieval.

source: Yu, Kraut, Kittur (2014) Distributed analogical idea generation (as cited by Chan et al. 2014)
finding: Cited as a crowd method for generating analogies by schema abstraction; not read.
numbers: none
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema-first route to analogues, consistent with Hope 2017.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs. ICLR
finding: The model proposes and solves analogous problems and reuses their results to fix its first solution. Reported gains across shortest-path, creative writing and agent planning.
numbers: Authors report average gains of 12 points (optimal shortest path), 13 points (human preference, creative writing), 15 points (ALFWorld task completion, 134 environments).
limits: Abstract-level numbers; analogous problems are same-type, i.e. near; no ablation of analogue distance found in the sections read.
agent_relevance: Another near-analogy success. Reusable lesson: solve analogues first, then revise from their solutions, citing the actual output (G2).
